Did you know that a cement kiln runs non-stop at more than 1,400 °C? That is why NASA satellites detect it almost every day… even though it is not a wildfire!
Did you know that oil flares burn the gas that comes out with crude oil? VIIRS sees them even at night, and the World Bank and NOAA use these data to measure global gas flaring. [Elvidge et al. 2016]

Did you know that on 13 November 1985 an eruption of Nevado del Ruiz triggered mudflows that buried the town of Armero, in Tolima? About 23,000 people died. Today the Colombian Geological Survey monitors it 24 hours a day, and NASA detects its heat from space. [SGC]
Did you know that coffee mills dry the beans by burning their own husks (called cisco)? That repeated heat shows up as a hotspot.
Did you know that Tolima is one of the largest rice producers in Colombia? Many mills burn rice husks to dry the grain, and satellites see that heat too. [Fedearroz]

It all starts in space.
NASA satellites Terra and Aqua fly at 705 kilometers, and Suomi NPP at 824 kilometers, circling the Earth from pole to pole about 14 times a day.
Their sensors sweep strips 2,330 and 3,040 kilometers wide, so Tolima, with 23,562 square kilometers, is seen about four times every day and night.
On board, infrared sensors measure the heat of every pixel.
A fire at about 800 degrees glows far brighter than its 30 degree surroundings in the 4 micrometer band.
VIIRS pixels are 375 meters, about 14 hectares, while MODIS pixels are 1 kilometer, about 100 hectares.
That is why VIIRS detects fires roughly seven times smaller.
The data are sent down to ground stations and processed by NASA's LANCE system.
In less than three hours each hotspot is published on FIRMS with its coordinates, date, time, confidence, and fire radiative power in megawatts, open to everyone.
We downloaded 66,192 detections from 2000 to 2025.
We clipped them to the 47 municipalities of Tolima with DANE boundaries, and removed 588 detections from the Nevado del Ruiz volcano, a cement plant, oil fields and rice mills.
Then we harmonized: since VIIRS sees about 5.9 times more than MODIS, older years are scaled so that all 26 years share the same scale.
Here is a real case.
Between the 12th and 22nd of September 2024, satellites detected 99 hotspots 11.4 kilometers east of the town of Natagaima, 95 kilometers south of Ibagué.
Together they released 1,558 megawatts, over a thermal footprint of about 1,022 hectares of savanna.
Sentinel-2 shows green vegetation on September 4th and a gray-brown burn scar on September 24th.
With 26 years of history we know what is normal for every week.
If a week goes far above that, especially in the dry season, the system could send an early warning to firefighters, CORTOLIMA and the national risk agency, before the fire gets out of control.
